fields.meta_title: What Is Worship? A Biblical Definition
fields.description: Worship is the response of the whole person to the worth of God — not just singing, but a life offered to him. Here is what worship means and how to do it.
fields.body_html:
Worship is the response of the whole person to the worth of God. The English word itself comes from “worth-ship” — to worship is to declare, with heart and life, that God is worthy, to give him the honour and love that match his infinite worth. We often shrink the word to mean singing on a Sunday, but in the Bible worship is far larger: it is the offering of everything we are to the God who made and redeemed us. Music is part of it, but so is obedience, service, generosity, and the ordinary faithfulness of daily life. In one sense everyone is a worshipper — the question is never whether we will worship, but what or whom. To understand worship is to understand what human beings are ultimately for, because we were made to worship — and we will worship something, whether the true God or a cheap substitute that can never satisfy the soul. “Worship the Lord in the splendor of holiness” (Psalm 29:2). Here is what worship really is, and how to give God the honour he alone deserves.

Worship is a response to who God is

True worship begins not with us but with God — with a sight of his greatness, holiness, and love. When Isaiah saw the Lord “high and lifted up,” and heard the angels cry “Holy, holy, holy is the Lord of hosts” (Isaiah 6:1–3), worship was the only possible response; he fell down undone and adoring. Worship is what happens when we see God as he is. The heavenly beings around his throne say it plainly: “Worthy are you, our Lord and God, to receive glory and honor and power, for you created all things” (Revelation 4:11).

This means worship is fundamentally God-centred, not us-centred. It is not primarily about what we get out of it — a good feeling, an emotional lift — but about giving God the honour due his name. When our eyes are filled with his worth, worship flows naturally, as water runs downhill. So the way to deepen worship is not to work up feelings but to look at God: to gaze on his character in Scripture, his works in creation, and above all his love at the cross, until the heart responds in adoration.

Worship is in spirit and in truth

Jesus gave the clearest definition of true worship to a stranger at a well. She was asking about the right place to worship, and he lifted her past the question entirely: “the hour is coming, and is now here, when the true worshipers will worship the Father in spirit and truth, for the Father is seeking such people to worship him. God is spirit, and those who worship him must worship in spirit and truth” (John 4:23–24).

Two things are required. Worship must be in spirit — from the heart, genuine and alive, not mere outward ritual or lip service. God is not impressed by performance that leaves the heart cold; he looks for reality. And worship must be in truth — according to who God actually is, as he has revealed himself, not according to our own imagination or preference. Heartfelt worship of a false idea of God is not true worship; and correct doctrine held with a cold heart is not worship either. The two belong together: real hearts and true knowledge, meeting in the presence of God.

All of life is worship

The New Testament expands worship far beyond any service or song. Paul writes, “I appeal to you therefore, brothers, by the mercies of God, to present your bodies as a living sacrifice, holy and acceptable to God, which is your spiritual worship” (Romans 12:1). Notice — the sacrifice is not an animal or a ceremony but our whole selves, our bodies, our daily lives, laid on the altar. Worship, in its fullest sense, is a life given to God.

This dissolves the false divide between “sacred” and “secular.” The Christian worships not only when singing but when working honestly, raising children faithfully, serving the poor, resisting temptation, and doing the smallest task “heartily, as for the Lord.” “Whether you eat or drink, or whatever you do, do all to the glory of God” (1 Corinthians 10:31). A meal, a workday, a kindness done in Jesus’ name — all of it becomes worship when offered to God. The whole of life is the arena of worship, and every moment an opportunity to declare his worth.

Worship engages the heart, the mind, and the body

Because we are whole persons, biblical worship engages all of us. It engages the emotions — the Psalms are full of joy, awe, longing, and even tears poured out before God. It engages the mind — we are to worship in truth, thinking rightly about God and letting the word of Christ dwell in us richly as we teach and admonish one another in song (Colossians 3:16). And it engages the body — Scripture speaks of kneeling, bowing, lifting hands, standing, and singing: “Oh come, let us worship and bow down; let us kneel before the Lord, our Maker!” (Psalm 95:6).

This wholeness guards us from two errors: a cold, cerebral religion that never moves the heart, and a shallow emotionalism that never engages the mind. God asks for both, and for the body too, because he made us as embodied souls. Worship is not merely something we think or feel; it is something we do, with everything we are.

Worship is offered together and alone

Worship has both a private and a corporate life, and we need both. In private, the believer worships alone — in the secret place of prayer, in unhurried time with God, in a heart that turns to him through the day. But God also calls his people to worship together, and there is a fullness in corporate worship that solitary devotion cannot supply. “Enter his gates with thanksgiving, and his courts with praise!” (Psalm 100:4) is addressed to a gathered people.

When believers assemble to praise God, hear his word, pray, and share the Lord’s table, they encourage one another and lift a united voice of praise that echoes the worship of heaven. To neglect gathered worship is to impoverish our own souls and to withhold from God the corporate honour he is due. So treasure both: the closet and the congregation, the quiet moment and the gathered church.

Worship changes the worshipper

One of the quiet wonders of worship is that it shapes us into the likeness of what we adore. We become like what we worship — for good or ill. Those who give their hearts to idols grow empty like them; those who worship the living God are slowly transformed into his image. Paul describes it: “And we all, with unveiled face, beholding the glory of the Lord, are being transformed into the same image from one degree of glory to another” (2 Corinthians 3:18). To gaze on God in worship is to be changed by him.

This means worship is never wasted time, even when it feels dry. Every act of turning our hearts to God, every song of praise, every offering of our lives, does a work in us we may not feel but that is real — softening the hard heart, warming the cold one, conforming us bit by bit to Christ. We do not worship in order to get something for ourselves, but God graciously gives us this: that in beholding him, we become like him. The person who worships God faithfully over a lifetime is slowly, surely remade.

Worship the Lord alone

Finally, worship belongs to God alone. When Satan offered Jesus the world in exchange for worship, Jesus answered, “You shall worship the Lord your God and him only shall you serve” (Matthew 4:10). Worship given to anything less than God — money, success, self, another person, even good things loved too much — is idolatry, and it always disappoints, because only God is worthy of the weight of our worship. The human heart is, as it has been called, a factory of idols; part of the Christian life is the steady work of tearing them down and giving God his rightful place.

So examine your worship. What actually commands your heart, your time, your treasure, your highest hopes? That is what you truly worship. The call of the gospel is to turn from every idol and give ourselves wholly to the God who gave himself for us — to “offer to God acceptable worship, with reverence and awe, for our God is a consuming fire” (Hebrews 12:28–29). Worship him in spirit and in truth, with your songs and with your life, and you will have found the very thing you were made for. For we were created to know and enjoy God, and worship is simply the heart doing what it was made to do — turning fully toward its Maker and finding, at last, that he is enough.
